solution.strong_distractor: b — '3rd century BCE to 8th century CE' tempts students who associate the Mathura school with the Mauryan period (3rd century BCE) as a starting point and the Arab/Turkish invasions (8th century CE) as an endpoint, both of which are plausible but incorrect temporal boundaries.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): '5th century BCE to 5th century CE' is too early a start and too early an end — the 5th century BCE predates the earliest Mathura sculptural evidence.
Eliminate option (b): '3rd century BCE to 8th century CE' confuses the Mauryan period as the Mathura school's origin; the school's distinct tradition begins around the 1st century BCE.
Eliminate option (c): '1st century CE to 12th century CE' is close but misses the pre-Kushana early phase beginning around the 1st century BCE.

Confirm option (d): '1st century BCE to 12th century CE' correctly captures the full span from the school's pre-Kushana indigenous beginnings through its post-Gupta continuation until the decline of Buddhism in North India.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap exploits the association of Mathura's 'greatness' with the Kushana period (1st–3rd century CE), leading students to start the school's chronology at the Kushana era rather than the pre-Kushana 1st century BCE phase. Similarly, the commonly cited 'end of ancient India' markers (Gupta collapse, Arab invasion) tempt students to prematurely end the school's timeline. The school's actual span — 1st century BCE to 12th century CE — is over a millennium of continuous artistic production.
solution.final_explanation:
The Mathura school's extraordinary longevity is one of its most remarkable characteristics, sustaining artistic production across a dozen centuries and multiple political regimes.

• Option (a) — 5th century BCE to 5th century CE: Incorrect. The 5th century BCE starting point predates the earliest identifiable Mathura sculptural tradition. The school's tradition emerged around the 1st century BCE with pre-Kushana Yaksha/Yakshi and early Jain images.
• Option (b) — 3rd century BCE to 8th century CE: Incorrect. While the Mauryan period (3rd century BCE) saw artistic activity in the broader region, the distinct Mathura school tradition begins around the 1st century BCE. The 8th century CE endpoint is also too early.
• Option (c) — 1st century CE to 12th century CE: Close but incomplete. This misses the pre-Kushana early phase (1st century BCE) when the indigenous sculptural vocabulary was being developed at Mathura before the Kushana period proper.
• Option (d) — 1st century BCE to 12th century CE: Correct. This span encompasses the early pre-Kushana phase (1st BCE), the Kushana florescence (1st–3rd CE), the Gupta classical phase (4th–6th CE), and the post-Gupta continuation until the decline of Buddhism in North India around the 12th century CE.

Value Addition:
• The 12th century CE decline correlates with the destruction of Buddhist monasteries and universities (Nalanda, Vikramashila) by Bakhtiyar Khilji's campaigns.
• The school's continuity across Kushana, Gupta, and post-Gupta periods demonstrates its deep embeddedness in Mathura's local economy and religious life.
• Post-12th century, the Hindu temple sculpture tradition absorbed many Mathura workshop conventions, ensuring a different form of continuity.

statement_analysis.statement: Mathura school — spotted red sandstone from Sikri quarries
statement_analysis.reason: Sikri red sandstone is the definitional material of the Mathura school throughout its history.

statement_analysis.statement: Amaravati school — cream-coloured Chunar sandstone
statement_analysis.reason: Amaravati used white limestone (sometimes called Palnad marble), not Chunar sandstone. Chunar sandstone belongs to the Sarnath school.

statement_analysis.statement: Gandhara school — grey schist stone and stucco
statement_analysis.reason: Grey schist and stucco are the defining materials of the Gandhara school in the northwest — this is standard knowledge.

statement_analysis.statement: Sarnath school — white limestone from the Krishna-Guntur region
statement_analysis.reason: Sarnath used Chunar sandstone (cream/buff), not white limestone. White limestone from the Krishna-Guntur region belongs to the Amaravati school.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify statements 1 and 3 as correct may think there are three correct statements if they also incorrectly accept either the Amaravati–Chunar or Sarnath–limestone pairing as partially plausible.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Mathura–Sikri red sandstone is correct — this is foundational knowledge.
Statement 2: Amaravati–Chunar sandstone is wrong; Chunar is Sarnath's material; Amaravati uses white limestone.
Statement 3: Gandhara–grey schist and stucco is correct.
Statement 4: Sarnath–white limestone from Krishna-Guntur is wrong; this description belongs to Amaravati; Sarnath uses Chunar sandstone. Total correct = 2 → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statements 2 and 4 execute a mutual swap — Amaravati's limestone is given to Sarnath, and Sarnath's Chunar sandstone is given to Amaravati. This is a double entity-swap that will trap students who know all four materials but struggle with the Sarnath–Amaravati pairing. The geographical clue in Statement 4 ('Krishna-Guntur region') actually helps a careful reader reject it for Sarnath — but only if they know that phrase belongs to Amaravati.
solution.final_explanation:
Matching sculptural schools to their primary materials is a high-frequency UPSC testing area.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Mathura → spotted red sandstone from Sikri (near Fatehpur Sikri). This is the school's defining material across its entire history.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Amaravati's material is white limestone (Palnad marble), not Chunar sandstone. Chunar sandstone (cream/buff) belongs to the Sarnath school. The swap here is between two schools whose materials are sometimes confused.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Gandhara → grey schist (a metamorphic stone from the northwestern mountains) AND stucco (a lime-plaster composite). Both were used extensively in Gandhara.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Sarnath's material is Chunar sandstone, not white limestone. The qualifier 'from the Krishna-Guntur region' should be an immediate alert — that geographic reference belongs to Amaravati, not Sarnath (which is near Varanasi).

Total correct = 2 → option (b).

Value Addition:
• The four major material-school pairings to memorize: Mathura=red sandstone (Sikri), Sarnath=buff sandstone (Chunar), Amaravati=white limestone (Palnad/Krishna-Guntur), Gandhara=grey schist+stucco.
• Chunar quarries are in present-day Mirzapur district of Uttar Pradesh, near Varanasi — geographically close to Sarnath.
• Grey schist's fine grain allowed Gandhara sculptors to achieve the detailed linear facial features characteristic of the school.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronological sequence of aniconic to iconic Buddhist art development
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places the Mathura/Gandhara iconic Buddha before Bharhut, which would mean iconic representation preceded aniconic — a student who doubts the chronology of Bharhut may select this.
elimination_logic: Bharhut stupa railings (2nd century BCE): one of the earliest Buddhist art sites, featuring purely aniconic representation — Buddha shown through symbols only. This comes first.
Sanchi Stupa I gateways (1st century BCE): another major aniconic site, also using symbolic representation — this comes after Bharhut but before iconic images.
First anthropomorphic (iconic) Buddha images at Mathura and Gandhara (approximately 1st century CE): this transition comes after the earlier aniconic traditions.
Correct sequence: Bharhut → Sanchi → Mathura/Gandhara iconic images → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets the Bharhut–Sanchi sequencing. Both are pre-iconic aniconic sites. Bharhut (Madhya Pradesh) predates Sanchi Stupa I's gateways — Bharhut is typically dated to the Shunga period (2nd century BCE) while Sanchi's famous toranas (gateways) are slightly later (1st century BCE to early 1st century CE). Students who know both are aniconic may correctly place them before Mathura iconic images but reverse their relative order.
solution.final_explanation:
The development of Buddhist art followed a clear trajectory from aniconic (symbolic) to iconic (anthropomorphic) representation.

Correct sequence: Bharhut stupa railings → Sanchi Stupa I gateways → First anthropomorphic Buddha images at Mathura and Gandhara.

• Bharhut stupa railings (2nd century BCE, Shunga period): Among the earliest Buddhist sculptural monuments. The Buddha is never shown in human form — represented by the Bodhi tree, footprints (Buddhapada), empty throne (sunya simhasana), the wheel (Dhamma Chakra), and the parasol. Jataka tales are depicted with the Buddha symbolized throughout.

• Sanchi Stupa I gateways/toranas (1st century BCE–1st century CE): The elaborately carved toranas at Sanchi continue the aniconic convention — the Buddha remains symbolically depicted even in narrative scenes showing events of his life. Slightly later than Bharhut.

• First anthropomorphic Buddha images at Mathura and Gandhara (approximately 1st century CE, Kushana period): The breakthrough to iconic representation. Both schools independently (or near-simultaneously) create the first human-form Buddha images.

Option (c) — Bharhut, then Sanchi, then Mathura/Gandhara iconic images — is correct.

Value Addition:
• Bharhut is in present-day Satna district of Madhya Pradesh; its sculptures are mostly in the Indian Museum, Kolkata.
• The toranas (gateways) of Sanchi are UNESCO World Heritage monuments; the stupa itself predates the toranas.
• The shift to iconic representation corresponds with the rise of Mahayana Buddhism, which emphasized devotional worship (bhakti) of the Buddha.

solution.concept_anchor: Colonial-era removal of Mathura sculptures and museum dispersal
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) about cultural property return treaties (such as UNESCO 1970 Convention) sounds plausible because students familiar with contemporary heritage law may correctly identify the legal framework but fail to recognize that the question asks specifically about the HISTORICAL role of colonial-era British officials in documenting (not just removing) Mathura sculptures.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes British officials in the 19th century systematically documenting and removing sculptures — this implicates colonial-era archaeological administration.
Eliminate option (b): the scenario describes systematic documentation AND removal by named officials, not random looting without institutional context.
Eliminate option (c): UNESCO 1970 Convention on cultural property illicit transfer is a 20th-century framework not applicable to 19th-century colonial activity described.
Eliminate option (d): the scenario describes archaeological administration and removal, not commercial art market activity.

Confirm option (a): Alexander Cunningham (Archaeological Survey of India founder) and F.S. Growse are the specifically named colonial-era figures associated with early Mathura sculpture documentation and the controversy over colonial removal — this is the historically accurate identification.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Option (c) extends the relevance of a real legal framework (UNESCO 1970 Convention) to a historical scenario it cannot apply to. Students with current affairs knowledge about cultural property repatriation may reach for option (c), applying a modern framework to a 19th-century context. The question tests whether students can correctly identify the colonial-era institutional actors (Cunningham, Growse) responsible for the historical phase of Mathura's documentation and the controversy surrounding sculpture removal.
solution.final_explanation:
A researcher studying the provenance of Mathura school sculptures in British and American museum collections traces their acquisition to systematic removal during the 19th century. Records show British colonial officials conducted excavations at sites including Kankali Tila and Katra mound, documented finds, and facilitated the transfer of sculptures to institutions in London, Boston, and Calcutta. The researcher identifies two officials by name as having been especially influential in early documentation and the subsequent dispersal of sculptures.

• Option (a) — Alexander Cunningham and F.S. Growse: Correct. These are the two specifically named colonial-era officials associated with early documentation of Mathura sculptures and the controversial removal of pieces. Cunningham founded the Archaeological Survey of India; Growse was a district collector who wrote about Mathura's antiquities. Their roles are documented in art-historical literature as part of the colonial-era phase of Mathura scholarship.
• Option (b) — Anonymous unauthorized looting without institutional support: Incorrect. The scenario specifically mentions systematic documentation by named officials — this was institutional, not random unauthorized activity.
• Option (c) — UNESCO 1970 Convention framework: Incorrect. This is a 20th-century legal instrument (adopted 1970) that cannot govern 19th-century colonial acquisitions. Applying it retrospectively is a scope-extension error.
• Option (d) — Private commercial art dealer network: Incorrect. While art dealers did play roles later, the scenario's description of systematic excavation, documentation, and institutional transfer points to state-sponsored colonial archaeological administration.

Value Addition:
• The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) was founded by Alexander Cunningham in 1861.
• The Indian Museum, Kolkata (founded 1814) was the primary repository for colonial-era Indian antiquities before the National Museum, New Delhi was established.
• The debate over repatriation of colonial-era acquisitions remains live: India has sought the return of several Mathura sculptures from foreign collections.

solution.concept_anchor: Halo design characteristics of Mathura school
solution.strong_distractor: b — The 'floral motifs and foliage' description sounds like it could belong to Mathura's decorative style, but this actually describes the Sarnath halo. Students who know Mathura halos are 'decorative' but don't know the specific design vocabulary may accept (b) as a Mathura feature.
elimination_logic: The grouping criterion: features genuinely associated with the halo/prabhavali in the Mathura school.
Geometric patterns — characteristic of Mathura halos; belongs.
Floral motifs and foliage patterns — characteristic of Sarnath halos (Gupta period), NOT Mathura; this is the odd one out.
Decorative beaded or jeweled borders — associated with Mathura's geometrically decorated halos; belongs.
Scalloped or flame-like outer edge — described in Mathura halo designs as part of the geometric-decorative vocabulary; belongs. Odd one out = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap: 'floral motifs and foliage' are indeed associated with Gupta-period halos — but specifically with Sarnath, not Mathura. Students who know the Gupta period saw more elaborate halo decoration may accept 'floral foliage' as a Gupta-Mathura feature, forgetting that this specific motif belongs to Sarnath. The distinction between Mathura's geometric halo and Sarnath's foliage-and-figures halo is the precise knowledge point being tested.
solution.final_explanation:
The prabhavali (halo or glory) behind the head of sacred images is a distinctive feature whose design varies between sculptural schools.

• Option (a) — Geometric decorative patterns: This IS a characteristic of Mathura halos. The prabhavali at Mathura features geometric designs — concentric bands, beaded circles, and repetitive geometric motifs. Belongs to the Mathura category.
• Option (b) — Elaborate floral motifs and foliage patterns with attendant figures: This does NOT belong to Mathura. This description precisely characterizes the Sarnath school's halo design — Sarnath's halos are famous for their lush foliage decoration and small attendant figures (vyalas, gandharvas). This is the odd one out.
• Option (c) — Beaded or jeweled border running around the outer edge: This is associated with Mathura's geometric halo decoration. Belongs.
• Option (d) — Scalloped or flame-bordered outer rim as part of the geometric vocabulary: Also within Mathura's geometric halo design tradition. Belongs.

Value Addition:
• The Sarnath halo's foliage-and-figures design represents a more naturalistic, organic aesthetic compared to Mathura's formal geometric approach.
• The prabhavali evolved over time: early Mathura halos are simpler geometric bands; later Mathura and Gupta halos became progressively more elaborate.
• In later medieval Hindu iconography, the prabhavali transformed into the elaborate flaming halo (prabhamandala) surrounding the entire body of deities.

solution.concept_anchor: Indigenous roots and anthropomorphic transition — Mathura's contributions

statement_analysis.statement: The pre-Mauryan and Mauryan Yaksha/Yakshi sculptural tradition provided the foundational visual vocabulary — including the treatment of voluminous forms, surface polish, and sensuous physicality — that Mathura sculptors adapted into Buddhist and Jain contexts.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the central argument for Mathura's indigenous character: the Yaksha/Yakshi tradition directly preceded and fed into the Mathura school's aesthetic, providing its visual vocabulary before any Buddhist iconographic demands existed.

statement_analysis.statement: The transition from aniconic to iconic Buddha representation facilitated the spread of Buddhism as a devotional religion, enabling lay communities to direct worship toward a concrete sacred image rather than an abstract symbol.
statement_analysis.reason: The creation of anthropomorphic Buddha images enabled a bhakti-like devotional relationship between lay worshippers and the image — this is the historical-religious significance of the aniconic-to-iconic transition, supported by art historians and religious scholars.

statement_analysis.statement: Mathura's indigenous sculptural tradition developed in response to the arrival of Buddhist missionaries from Gandhara, who introduced the concept of anthropomorphic sacred images to the Mathura region.
statement_analysis.reason: This reverses the actual relationship. Mathura's tradition is indigenous and predates any Gandhara influence; moreover, Mathura independently developed (or co-developed) anthropomorphic Buddha images. Gandhara missionaries did not introduce anthropomorphism to Mathura — the causation runs the other way, or more accurately, both schools developed independently.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who doubt Statement 3's claim may still consider it might be partially true (given Kushana-period connections between Mathura and Gandhara) and end up selecting all three as correct — making option (d) the primary trap.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Correct — Yaksha/Yakshi → Mathura visual vocabulary is a standard art-historical claim with strong scholarly backing.
Statement 2: Correct — the devotional significance of iconic Buddha images and its role in Buddhism's spread is historically supported.

Statement 3: Incorrect — this reverses causation; Mathura's tradition is indigenous and predates Gandhara influence; the 'Gandhara missionaries introduced anthropomorphism' claim is a fabricated reversal.
Only statements 1 and 2 are correct → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a reversed-causation trap. It takes the genuine historical connection between Mathura and Gandhara (both under Kushana patronage, both developing anthropomorphic imagery) and fabricates a directional relationship where Gandhara 'introduced' the concept to Mathura. This is wrong: Mathura's indigenous tradition is older, and the scholarly consensus is that both schools developed anthropomorphic imagery independently or near-simultaneously. Presenting Gandhara as the source and Mathura as the recipient reverses the actual relationship between the foreign-influenced and indigenous schools.
solution.final_explanation:
The foundations of the Mathura school's significance rest on two interconnected arguments: its indigenous roots and its role in the aniconic-to-iconic transition.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Yaksha/Yakshi tradition is the direct ancestral vocabulary for Mathura sculpture. The sensuous three-dimensional forms, high surface polish, and monumental scale of Yaksha/Yakshi figures from the Mauryan period fed directly into Mathura's Buddhist and Jain sculptural aesthetic. This indigeneity is what distinguishes Mathura from the foreign-influenced Gandhara school.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The creation of the anthropomorphic Buddha image had profound religious consequences. It enabled bhakti-type devotion — lay worship directed at a visible, tangible sacred form — which accelerated Buddhism's spread across Asia. The iconic image became the medium through which Buddhism became a mass devotional religion rather than an elite philosophical system.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: This inverts the actual relationship. Mathura's tradition is indigenous, pre-Buddhist in its roots, and developed anthropomorphic imagery independently. The claim that Gandhara missionaries 'introduced' anthropomorphic concepts to Mathura has no scholarly support and contradicts the evidence of Mathura's pre-Kushana indigenous tradition.

Value Addition:
• The bhakti element entering Buddhism through iconic worship later paralleled the Bhakti movement's entry into Hinduism — devotional image worship became a pan-Indian religious phenomenon.
• Mathura's Yaksha/Yakshi tradition is sometimes called 'proto-Buddhist art' to emphasize its role as the visual precursor.
• The Mauryan period Yaksha from Parkham (near Mathura) is one of the earliest large-scale stone sculptures from the region, predating any Buddhist art there.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Assigning Kankali Tila to Buddhist finds is the most probable error. Students who associate Mathura overwhelmingly with Buddhism may assume all major mounds at Mathura yielded Buddhist material, not distinguishing the specifically Jain character of Kankali Tila.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits the near-universal association of Mathura with Buddhism. Students who have not memorized the specific site-religion pairings will default to associating all major Mathura excavation mounds with Buddhist finds. solution.final_explanation:
Mathura's archaeological landscape includes sites associated with three different religious traditions, and knowing which site belongs to which tradition is a precision-knowledge test.

• Option (a) — Kankali Tila: Buddhist stupa remains; Mat village: Jain dedicatory plaques: Incorrect on both counts. Kankali Tila is Jain, not Buddhist. Mat village yielded Kushana royal portrait sculptures, not Jain dedicatory plaques.
• Option (b) — Kankali Tila: Buddhist sculptural finds from the Kushana period: Incorrect. This is the main entity-swap trap. Kankali Tila is definitively the Jain site — it yielded early Jain stone images, Ayagapatas (Jain votive tablets), and Jain stupa remains.
• Option (c) — Kankali Tila: Jain sculptures including Ayagapatas: Correct. This is the accurate identification. Kankali Tila in Mathura is the principal Jain archaeological site, excavated to yield the earliest corpus of Jain stone sculpture and the unique Ayagapata dedicatory slabs.
• Option (d) — Government Museum, Mathura: exclusively houses Kushana royal portrait sculptures: Incorrect. The Government Museum, Mathura is the largest general repository of Mathura school sculptures across all periods and religions — not limited to Kushana royal material.

Value Addition:
• Kankali Tila excavations were conducted partly by the Archaeological Survey of India and partly by A.A. Führer in the late 19th century.
• Ayagapatas from Kankali Tila are now housed in the Government Museum, Mathura and the State Museum, Lucknow.
• The name 'Kankali Tila' derives from a Kankali Devi temple on the mound — reflecting the multi-religious stratigraphy of the site.

solution.final_explanation:
Mathura's unique character as a multi-religious sculptural center is explained by its geographic and economic position.

Assertion (A): Correct. Mathura is distinctive in Indian art history for simultaneously producing major sculptural traditions for all three of India's great institutional religions — Buddhism, Jainism, and Hinduism — within the same workshops and historical period. Buddhist stupas and Bodhisattva images, Jain Tirthankara figures and Ayagapatas, and early Hindu images of Vishnu, Shiva, and Krishna were all produced at Mathura.

Reason (R): Correct. Mathura's geographic position at the junction of major trade arteries — including the Uttarapatha (northern highway connecting the northwest to eastern India) and routes connecting the Gangetic plain to western and southern India — made it one of ancient India's most cosmopolitan urban centers. Merchants, pilgrims, monks, and artisans from multiple religious communities converged there.

Causal relationship: R directly and sufficiently explains A. The convergence of multiple religious communities at Mathura — enabled by its trade-route crossroads location — created patronage demand for Buddhist, Jain, and Hindu art simultaneously. Without this geographic-commercial factor, the multi-religious character of Mathura's output would be inexplicable.

Value Addition:
• Mathura's position on the Uttarapatha also explains why Kushana rulers — who controlled the silk road trade — chose it as their southern capital.
• The same trade-route logic explains Nalanda's rise as a multi-disciplinary Buddhist university — it too was situated on a major trade corridor.
• Krishna's mythological birthplace identity added a specifically Hindu devotional overlay to Mathura's already pluralistic religious landscape.

statement_analysis.reason: This accurately describes the Kushana-to-Gupta stylistic transition at Mathura: from the powerful, sensuous Kushana Buddha to the more spiritually refined, serene Gupta Buddha with elaborated floral elements in the halo.

statement_analysis.reason: Despite both being Gupta-period schools, Sarnath and Mathura retain distinct regional styles — most visibly in drapery (Sarnath's plain robe vs. Mathura's string-fold), halo design (Sarnath's foliage vs. Mathura's geometric), and material (Chunar vs. Sikri sandstone).

statement_analysis.reason: While both schools flourished under Kushana patronage, they did not decline simultaneously. Mathura continued its tradition through the Gupta period (4th–6th CE) and beyond; the Gandhara school's trajectory was different, but Mathura's is not simply 'post-Kushana decline' — it had a major second florescence under the Guptas.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Statement 1 is clearly correct, and students looking for incorrect statements will not select it. But students uncertain about whether Gupta halos at Mathura had 'floral motifs' (versus purely geometric) may incorrectly mark Statement 1 as not correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The Kushana-to-Gupta transition at Mathura involving increased serenity and floral halo elements is correctly described — this is correct, do NOT select.

Statement 2: 'Stylistically indistinguishable' and 'erased all regional differences' are both wrong — Sarnath and Mathura retain distinct drapery, halo, and material differences even in the Gupta period.
Statement 3: The claim that both schools 'declined simultaneously after Kushana fall' is wrong — Mathura had a major Gupta-period florescence after the Kushana era, not a decline.
Both statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the conflation technique — merging the distinct Sarnath and Mathura regional styles into a single 'unified Gupta imperial style.' Students who know both are 'Gupta-period schools' may not immediately challenge the 'indistinguishable' claim without precise knowledge of the halo-drapery-material differences. Statement 3 compounds this with a temporal-swap: Mathura's post-Kushana trajectory involved a GUPTA FLORESCENCE, not a simultaneous decline with Gandhara. These two errors together test whether students can hold the distinct trajectories of multiple schools in mind simultaneously.
solution.final_explanation:
The Gupta period represents both the maturation of Mathura's tradition and a phase where its distinctiveness from Sarnath must be carefully maintained.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Gupta-period Mathura Buddha shows clear stylistic evolution from the Kushana phase — the robust physicality gives way to serene spirituality, drapery becomes more refined, and the halo incorporates floral elements alongside its characteristic geometric patterns. This transition is well-documented.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Despite both being Gupta-period products, Sarnath and Mathura are NOT stylistically indistinguishable. Three clear markers persist: (i) drapery — Sarnath's unmodeled plain robe vs. Mathura's string-fold; (ii) halo — Sarnath's foliage-and-figures vs. Mathura's geometric; (iii) material — Chunar sandstone vs. Sikri red sandstone. The 'unified Gupta style' claim is a conflation error.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Mathura's post-Kushana history was one of renewal under Gupta patronage, not simultaneous decline with Gandhara. The Gupta period (4th–6th century CE) was Mathura's second major florescence. Gandhara's trajectory (affected by different political dynamics in the northwest) was distinct from Mathura's.

Value Addition:
• The Gupta empire's artistic patronage was not monolithic — it supported regional schools (Mathura, Sarnath, Ajanta) that retained distinct characters.
• The Gandhara school's decline is associated with the Sasanian Persian pressure from the west and the Huna invasions from the north — different from Mathura's pressures.
• Post-Gupta Mathura shows a third phase: increasing ornamentation, greater rigidity, absorption into the emerging Hindu temple sculpture tradition.
